tracks.title: One binary knows who's listening
tracks.text: Lesson seven point one — modes. This one is a sub-lesson, under wbx — the command line for living software. One binary… knows who's listening. The same wbx command serves your terminal, your CI script, and your agents. And here's the surprise — it is not three tools. It is not even three code paths. It is one module, about two hundred lines, that every single verb flows through… once. [curious] A mode is just the manner wbx adopts for its audience. What the tool does never changes. Only how it speaks. This lesson is the exact rules… so you can write the retry loop today.

tracks.title: The tool that hangs in CI
tracks.text: First — the tool that hangs in CI. You know this tool. It runs fine on your laptop. You wire it into a build job… and the build sits there for twenty minutes. [sighs] Silently. Waiting at a yes-or-no prompt nobody will ever answer. You fix that — and now your logs are full of color escape codes the log viewer can't read. And when something finally fails, it exits with code one. For everything. Always. With a paragraph of prose you have to grep through to find out why. The usual industry answer is to ship two things. First, a command line, for humans. Second, a separate kit or API, for machines. And they drift apart — the flag the command line grew last week isn't in the kit yet. But an ecosystem with one tool — one binary on the laptop, in CI, and inside the engine — can't take that fork. So wbx solves it with manners… not forks. [chuckles] The work is one code path. The audience is decided once… at the very end.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A mode is the manner wbx adopts for its audience — one of three. First, Human. Second, Agent. Third, Json. Chosen once per run. Three manners… one code path. The command does identical work and returns the same value. The mode decides only how that value is spoken. It's a single enum in the code, and the spec frames it in four words — one switch, three ways to set it, sensible default. And the rule underneath is that human mode should be dumb-simple. The tool does the work. A learning curve is treated as a bug. [curious] The same instinct, pointed the other way, is what makes the machine modes trustworthy.

tracks.title: Eleven lines that decide
tracks.text: Now — eleven lines that decide. The whole split begins in one function, called detect, and the order of its checks is the entire contract. Picture a ladder, top to bottom, first match wins. Step one: was the json flag passed? If yes — Json mode, the envelope. If no, step two: is the agent flag set, or the environment variable WBX_AGENT equal to one? If yes — Agent mode, plain text, no prompts. If no, step three: is standard output actually a terminal? If yes — Human mode, the landing, color, prompts. And if none of those fire — piped, redirected, no terminal at all — the fallback is Agent. [curious] And that last rung is the important one. When wbx can't tell who's listening, it does not assume a human is standing there to answer a prompt. The safe failure for an unknown caller is silence and plain text… never a hang. A pipe is agent-by-default precisely because a pipe might be a CI runner with no keyboard attached. The terminal test, by the way, is one standard-library call — no extra dependency. And one honest nit. The variable must be exactly the string one. WBX_AGENT equals true… does nothing. The check is literal. Set it to one… or don't set it. Picture the same verb, four ways. wbx status, on a terminal — you get a landing and a start-here menu. wbx status piped into cat — agent mode, a structured body, no menu, no color. WBX_AGENT equals one then wbx status — agent manners, on a terminal. And wbx dash dash json status — the envelope itself. One nice touch — the agent landing splices the whole verb tree into the health report. One call… and an agent knows both the system's health and its entire surface.

tracks.title: One channel, rendered once
tracks.text: One channel… rendered once. Detection is cheap because of a discipline upstream of it. Every command in wbx returns a single string. And the main function is the only thing that renders. Picture the shape of main — it's tiny. First, it calls detect to choose the mode. Second, it rebuilds the verb name. Third, it runs the one verb, which hands back either an okay-string or an error. And then — only then — it renders that result exactly once. Okay goes to render-okay. Error goes to render-error. That's the whole seam. The spec calls it one output channel, and credits it with making the entire mode model a mechanical refactor… rather than a rewrite. Because the verb already produced one string, adding three manners meant adding one renderer at the exit — not editing every command. Picture the path as a relay. You, or an agent, type wbx toolkit audit dash dash json. Clap parses it and picks the verb. The run function does the real work and hands back either an okay-string… or an error. Then the mode layer renders that result once — output to standard out, any hint to standard error, and the exit code set. Nothing branches on audience until that final hand-off. Two supporting details. First — the verb rebuilder reads the raw arguments, skips the flags, takes the first real word, and for group verbs like toolkit and deploy it reaches in for the sub-verb too. So the envelope reports toolkit audit… not just toolkit. There's a test that pins exactly that. Second — the few commands that truly need different content per audience, like doctor, take a human boolean and shape their data accordingly. Prose for people… a structured body for agents. Everything else is identical work, spoken three ways.

tracks.title: One shape for every outcome
tracks.text: One shape… for every outcome. In Json mode, success and failure share one predictable skeleton — the thing a script parses once and trusts forever. Success is — ok true, the verb, and data. Failure is — ok false, the verb, and an error object holding a code, a message, a hint, and a retryable flag. Let me read you a real failure, with no engine reachable. The command — WBX_ENGINE_URL pointed at port one, then wbx dash dash json rt status. And back comes — ok false, verb rt status, error code three, message a tcp connect error on one-two-seven-dot-zero-dot-zero-dot-one port one, hint — no engine reachable, start one with wbx deploy local. And retryable… true. Then you check the exit code… and it's three. The envelope and the exit code agree. [excited] Three things in there earn a closer look. First — the data field is embedded structurally when it can be. The renderer tries to parse the command's output as json; if it's already json, it nests it as real structure; only if it's plain text does it wrap it as a text field. You never get json trapped inside a string when real json was available. Second — the retryable flag is computed… not hand-set. It's true exactly when the code is three, engine, or six, conflict — the two failures a retry can plausibly fix. Third — note where the envelope rides. Even on failure, it goes to standard out… not standard error. Because in Json mode, the envelope is the answer — success or not.

tracks.title: Classify, the honest heuristic
tracks.text: Classify… the honest heuristic. This one's a depth-rung — skippable on a first listen, essential if you're writing the retry loop. The exit codes are a small fixed set. Zero for okay. Two for a usage error — and that one is owned by the argument parser, not by wbx; there's a test pinning it. Then a handful of typed failures — three for engine, four for not-found, five for verify, six for conflict, seven for auth. And everything that doesn't match falls to one, the catch-all. So how does a code get chosen? Today, by a function called classify — and the source is blunt about what it is. A heuristic, over the lowercased text of the error chain… until errors carry typed codes. The contract is the code… not the text. [curious] That sentence is the most important thing here for a script author. You branch on the number. You never parse the message. Picture the mapping as five rules. First — if the text mentions connection refused, or tcp connect, or no runtime — that's code three, and the hint says start an engine with wbx deploy local. Second — four-oh-four, or not found, or no such file — code four, and the hint names the list verbs so you can see what does exist. Third — signature, or integrity — code five, re-sign with wbx sign. Fourth — four-oh-nine, or conflict — code six, the state moved underneath you, re-read and retry. Fifth — four-oh-one, or forbidden — code seven, fix your token. And the verdict of all that — each failure class names the command that fixes it. And the two retryable ones are three and six. A four means enumerate what exists. A five means re-sign. A seven means fix your token… and never retry blindly.

tracks.title: Manners versus format
tracks.text: Manners… versus format. This is the sharpest distinction on the page, and the one most people get wrong. Piping wbx does not give you the json envelope. A pipe selects Agent mode — which is manners. No prompts, no color, plain text. The envelope is a format. And you get it only by asking — dash dash json. So — Agent mode is how wbx behaves. Json mode is what it emits. There's a contract test whose entire job is to prove that a piped command's output never starts with the ok-brace. Let me give you the three columns as a story instead of a grid. On prompts — Human mode prompts you; Agent and Json… never. On color — Human mode is promised it; Agent and Json emit none. On success — Human gets a landing and a menu; Agent gets the plain string; Json gets the envelope. And on the hint — and this is the subtle part — the hint goes to whoever can act on it, in the channel they actually read. A human gets it on standard error, right under the error, where their eyes already are. An agent in plain mode gets only the bare error line — no hint, because plain agent output is for piping, not advising. And Json mode carries the hint structurally, inside the envelope, so a program can act on it. Same hint… three deliveries. Or none — when none would just be noise.

tracks.title: What only humans get
tracks.text: What only humans get. Another depth-rung — the two features that live entirely behind the mode gate. Some things are luxuries a machine must never reach. wbx keeps two of them, and both are gated so hard that agent mode literally cannot trip over them. The first is the picker. It prints its menu to standard error and reads one line from standard in. Its doc comment is a warning to future maintainers — human mode only, agent mode never reaches this. It has exactly one real call site — wbx deploy init, run bare on a terminal, which asks — engine place, where does this run? Option one, local — a container on this machine, cloud-identical. Option two, cloud — fly dot io, under your own account. Now pipe that same command with standard in closed… and there is no hang. It instantly takes the local default, writes the deployment file, and tells you — wrote deployment dot org, local, edit it then run wbx deploy apply. [chuckles] And the gate is enforced twice over. On a non-terminal the picker is never called… and the in-sandbox build of the picker always returns the default no matter what. The sandboxed wbx physically cannot prompt. The second luxury is the next-hint — verb chaining, printed to standard error, human only. After a successful deploy init on a terminal, the output grows a tail an agent never sees — next, wbx deploy apply, converge to what you declared. Picture the chain left to right, as a guided path. Finish a build, and wbx whispers — now bundle. Bundle, and it says — now sign. Sign, and it offers two ways forward — verify it… or deploy the workbook. Init a deploy, and the chain points you to apply, then to status and logs. An agent gets none of this… and wants none of it. [chuckles] It already knows where it's going.

tracks.title: The contract is a test suite
tracks.text: The contract… is a test suite. None of this is documentation-only. Every promise on this page has an assertion behind it, in one test file. That file is the real contract; the prose is just a tour of it. Let me walk the promises and the tests that pin them. First — success is one envelope, ok true, verb and data present. Second — a not-found exits four, and the envelope's code is four, so they agree. Third — a pipe is plain text; its output never starts with the ok-brace. Fourth — deploy init with standard in closed never prompts, and writes the file. Fifth — the WBX prefix beats the older WB prefix when both are set. Sixth — open on a missing path exits four. Seventh — a bare wbx is a landing, not a usage error, and exits zero. And eighth — the classify table itself maps to the contract codes. [excited] The verdict — the most agent-hostile failures are each a named, failing-if-broken test. A hang on a closed standard in. An envelope that disagrees with its own exit code. A pipe that vomits json you didn't ask for. The never-prompts one is the strongest — it runs deploy init with standard in set to null, asserts the command succeeds, and asserts the deployment file exists on disk afterward. Closed standard in, no hang, file written… proven, not promised. Two more shape everyday use. Doctor always exits zero, even with no engine — a health check must not fail the shell. And the author verbs accept a dash for standard in — echo a headline, pipe it into wbx lint dash, and you get back an empty list.

tracks.title: Where the seam is honest
tracks.text: Where the seam is honest. The mode model is small and tested — but it isn't finished, and pretending otherwise would undercut the whole point of a contract. Five honest edges. First — classify is string-matching, for now. Typed error codes are the future; the code is the contract today. Which is exactly why you branch on the number, never on the message. Second — exit code two belongs to the argument parser, not to classify. A deliberate boundary. Third — code one is the catch-all. Treat it as unknown… not as a specific failure. Fourth — the agent variable must be exactly the string one. Not true, not yes — the literal one. Fifth — the failure envelope rides standard out, not standard error, so a single parse covers both outcomes. And one thing we won't claim — whether human mode paints color and tables today. The spec promises that experience, and the pickers and the landing are real and tested. The color, we won't overstate. What we will stand behind, fully, is the tested half — agent mode emits no color, ever. That's the half a script depends on… and that half is law.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Why does piping give me plain text and not json? Because a pipe selects Agent mode — manners, not format. No prompts, no color. The envelope is a separate request — add dash dash json. Is the error message stable enough to parse? No — and you shouldn't. Branch on the code in the envelope, or the exit code in a shell. The code is the contract; the text is for humans. How do I force human manners inside a pipe? You can't. There's an agent flag and a json flag… but no human flag. Human mode is reached only by a real terminal. That's intentional — the human luxuries are exactly the things that misbehave when nobody's watching. What is retryable computed from? The exit code, nothing else. True exactly when the code is three or six. Never hand-set, so it can't drift out of sync. And — does the old WB prefix still work? Yes. The canonical prefix is WBX; the older WB is accepted as a fallback. When both are set… WBX wins. A test points each at a different port and proves it.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's modes. Not an agent flavor of the tool… one tool that decides who's listening, on its last line, and speaks accordingly. Detection is a single stdlib call. The work is one code path. The manner is at the edge. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under wbx — lesson seven — the command line this seam lives inside. Read that one for the verb families and the exit-code table this page proves. And from there, follow the seam outward — to agents, the consumers agent mode serves… and to the engine that code three tells you to start.
